chapter: Working for the King and Ranshaw families
title: Languages at the King household and the Ranshaw family
summary: Working for Mrs. King she picked up Spanish and French from teachers who gave classes; she talks about Gladys Ranshaw and the judge she served.

story.theme_name: Growing up and learning music: family, first instruments, teachers
story.community_name: Where I came from: parents, siblings and birth

blocks.x: Well, it's the language that I could read with more facilité, you know. Yes. But I read because, you see, old Mrs. W. W. King, Grace King. Her mother? Huh? Grace King's mother? Grace King's mother. I worked there. And there they used to have classes every three, about four days in the week. One day it would be Capitán de Chivarria, that was for the Spanish. And nothing but Spanish. And they speak it to me and I dig it like a little young crazy thing, you know. I wasn't twenty years old. Then one day it was Herman Gassner. You must have, Herman Gassner, he teaches at Hueline. But this Herman Gassner that's there, must be his grandson. But old Herman Gassner used to teach at Miss King, Capitaine de Chivarria, Miss Guigar, Madame Gérard, and, how do you call them? Charles Guayari.
And which language did Guayari teach?

Who was that lady that was voted, you know, she got some honor about two years ago, that she was voted the best teacher of the year. Do you remember she sent you her orchids that time? Do you remember she? I don't remember.
Was she from Newcomb? From Newcomb, yes. Could that be her?
Gracie K, Gracie, Ranshaw, Gladys Ranshaw. That's who it was, Gladys Ranshaw. Gladys Ranshaw, yes.
And you worked for them too, did you? So the more born. I don't remember the lady, how she looked.
Maybe she don't teach no more now. No, she's retired, I guess. Retired.
But you worked for them then too, did you?
I've been in that family since her sister, which is dead now, was 14 years old.
Is she related to Miss LeBreton? Huh? Is she related to Miss LeBreton? Who? Gladys Ranshaw?
Well, that's her sister. I see.

George Ranshaw had, I believe, nine girls and two boys. Ah, but that was a man. Worth imitating. He had such nice manners, so quiet, so serious, so charitable. Oh, I liked the judge very much. Stayed with him till he left this earth.
